source: Marcura Maritime Scope 3 Strategy Report, Sections 1, 9, and 16
problem: Maritime Scope 3 data is fragmented across procurement, suppliers, invoices, shipments, and emissions sources.
opportunity: Marcura is well positioned to enter the maritime Scope 3 emissions technology market, but not as a general-purpose carbon accounting vendor. The opportunity that matters is narrower and more defensible: no company reviewed in this assessment — including the market's most mature infrastructure provider — has built a maritime-native procurement, supplier engagement, and workflow layer on top of carbon calculation. That gap is where Marcura's existing position in the maritime industry becomes a genuine competitive asset rather than a starting-from-zero disadvantage. Recommendation: License the general-purpose calculation engine and emission-factor database. Partner for vessel-level, AIS-based emissions precision. Build the maritime procurement taxonomy, supplier engagement workflow, and audit trail — the layer where no competitor currently operates and where Marcura's industry position is most defensible. This report answers five questions in sequence: whether the market is attractive enough to enter; who the real competitors are and where value concentrates in the technology stack; how Marcura should position itself against them; what the optimal Build, Buy, and Partner allocation looks like; and what could break the recommendation. Each section builds directly on the one before it, and the final recommendation is stress-tested against the most plausible ways it could fail.
strategic_response: License the calculation engine and factor database. Partner for vessel-level AIS precision. Build the maritime procurement, supplier engagement, and audit-trail layer. Do not attempt to build a general-purpose, independently audited calculation engine — that problem has already been solved by the market, and re-solving it would consume years without adding differentiation.
outcome: Marcura should enter the maritime Scope 3 technology market, conditional on confirming genuine maritime procurement, supplier, and invoice data access, and on shipping the initial release as an embedded workflow feature rather than a standalone platform. The market is regulation-driven and time-bound: three converging IMO and EU mandates, high buyer power favoring embedded incumbents, and rising but not yet consolidated rivalry together create a real but narrowing window. No competitor reviewed occupies the specific position Marcura is positioned to fill — maritime-specialised, workflow-embedded, and built around procurement and supplier engagement rather than calculation alone. That recommendation holds under stress testing against the most plausible competitive responses, with two explicit conditions that shape how, not whether, Marcura should proceed.
conclusion: The maritime Scope 3 technology market rewards depth of maritime domain expertise more than depth of carbon-calculation infrastructure. General-purpose providers have already solved the calculation and standards-compliance problem to a level Marcura should license rather than replicate; maritime-relevant point solutions have solved vessel-level precision to a level Marcura should partner for rather than rebuild. What remains unaddressed — a maritime-native procurement taxonomy, supplier engagement workflow, and embedded audit trail — is precisely the layer where an established maritime technology provider holds a structural advantage that no reviewed competitor can easily replicate. The opportunity is real, time-bound, and conditional. Proceeding on the terms set out in this report — licensing the commoditized infrastructure, partnering for specialised vessel-level precision, and building the maritime workflow layer as an embedded feature within existing customer relationships — gives Marcura a credible path to a defensible position in a market that, on present evidence, no competitor has yet claimed.
